title: In the Mood for Love
why: Two neighbours in 1960s Hong Kong discover their spouses are having an affair, and slowly fall for each other without acting on it. It is one of the most beautiful films ever made, with its slow motion, cheongsam dresses and repeated waltz theme. It shows how much can be said through restraint.
watchFor: How often the characters are framed through doorways, mirrors and corridors, as if we are spying on them.
The repeated music and slow motion, and how they turn ordinary moments into memory.
after: What does the film suggest about the cost of always doing the 'proper' thing?

title: Portrait of a Lady on Fire
why: A painter is hired to secretly paint a young woman's wedding portrait on a remote Breton island in the 1770s. It is a love story about looking and being looked at, filmed like a series of paintings. Almost no men appear, which quietly changes how we see everything.
watchFor: Who is looking at whom, and how that shifts during the film.
The use of near silence, and the two moments when music finally arrives.
after: How does it change a portrait when the subject looks back at the artist? Think of a portrait from your art cards.

title: Atlantics
why: In Dakar, construction workers who have not been paid set off across the sea for Spain, and the women they leave behind begin to change. Part love story, part ghost story, part protest about migration and labour. Diop was the first Black woman director in competition at Cannes.
watchFor: The ocean, which appears again and again, almost as a character.
How the film moves from realism into the supernatural, and why it might need to.
after: What drives people to risk everything to migrate? Think about Senegal's 'teranga' and what home means.

title: If Beale Street Could Talk
why: From the director of Moonlight, adapted from James Baldwin's novel. A young couple in 1970s Harlem have their future upended when he is falsely accused of a crime. It is tender, warm and heartbreaking, and its colours and close-ups are stunning.
watchFor: The characters looking straight into the camera, and how that makes you feel.
The rich colour of clothes and rooms, and how it carries the love story.
after: Baldwin wrote that nothing can be changed until it is faced. What does this film ask its audience to face?

title: Past Lives
why: Two childhood friends from Seoul are separated when one emigrates, and reconnect decades later in New York. A quiet film about the lives we did not live and the person migration made us into. It earned two Oscar nominations, including Best Picture.
watchFor: The Korean idea of 'in-yun', fate between people across lifetimes, and how the film uses it.
The long silences in the final scenes.
after: Who would you be if you had grown up somewhere else?

title: Aftersun
why: A Scottish woman remembers a holiday in Turkey with her young father when she was eleven. On the surface it is a sunny package holiday; underneath, it slowly reveals his struggle with depression. A debut film that quietly devastates many viewers.
watchFor: The camcorder footage and what it shows compared with what it hides.
How the adult daughter's memories break into the past.
after: How well do we ever know the inner lives of the people who raised us?

title: Roma
why: A year in the life of a live-in domestic worker for a middle-class family in 1970s Mexico City, drawn from Cuarón's own childhood. Shot in black and white, it gives a usually invisible woman the full weight of an epic. Politics and history unfold in the background.
watchFor: The long, slow camera pans that let you look around rooms and streets.
How the student protests of 1971 appear at the edges of the story.
after: Whose labour makes your daily life possible without you noticing it?

title: Parasite
why: A poor family cons its way into working for a rich one, and things spiral. Funny, tense and shocking, it was the first non-English language film to win the Oscar for Best Picture. A sharp look at class and inequality.
watchFor: Stairs and levels: who lives up, who lives down, and where water flows.
The 'smell' that keeps being mentioned, and what it represents.
after: How would a socialist and a free-market thinker each explain what goes wrong in this film?

title: Shoplifters
why: A struggling family in Tokyo survives by petty theft, and takes in a neglected little girl they find in the cold. Gentle and warm, then gradually unsettling. It won the Palme d'Or at Cannes.
watchFor: Small acts of care in a cramped, messy home.
How your view of the family changes in the last act.
after: What makes a family: blood, law, or choice?

title: A Separation
why: A middle-class couple in Tehran split over whether to leave Iran, setting off a chain of misunderstandings with their carer's family. Every character is partly right and partly wrong. It won the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film.
watchFor: How the film withholds a key moment so you judge without full information.
Differences of class and religious belief between the two families.
after: Which character did you side with first, and did that change? Try the debate question on this one.

title: Timbuktu
why: Jihadist militants take over Timbuktu and ban music, football and more. The film shows everyday resistance with dignity, beauty and even humour. Sissako avoids easy villains, which makes it more powerful.
watchFor: The football match played without a ball.
The wide desert landscapes against the closed-in rules of the occupiers.
after: How do ordinary people resist without weapons?

title: Daughters of the Dust
why: In 1902, a Gullah family on an island off South Carolina prepares to move north. It was the first feature by an African American woman to get a general release in the US. Its dreamlike images later inspired Beyoncé's Lemonade.
watchFor: The white dresses against the sea and sand, and how they echo through the film.
The narration by an unborn child.
after: What is kept, and what is lost, when a family leaves its home for a better life?

title: Cléo from 5 to 7
why: A young singer wanders Paris while waiting for the results of a medical test, in almost real time. A key film of the French New Wave by one of its few women directors. It moves from being looked at to looking.
watchFor: How Cléo changes when she takes off her wig and fashionable clothes.
Mirrors, and the moment she stops looking into them.
after: Simone de Beauvoir wrote that one becomes a woman. How does Cléo 'become' someone different over two hours?

title: Tokyo Story
why: An elderly couple visit their grown-up children in Tokyo, who are too busy for them. Often voted one of the greatest films ever made. Simple, calm and deeply moving about family, time and change in post-war Japan.
watchFor: The low camera height, as if you are sitting on the tatami floor.
The 'pillow shots' of empty streets and chimneys between scenes.
after: What do we owe our parents as they get older?

title: Bicycle Thieves
why: In post-war Rome, a man's bicycle, which he needs for his new job, is stolen, and he and his son search the city for it. A landmark of Italian neorealism, made with non-professional actors on real streets. Simple, honest and unforgettable.
watchFor: The relationship between father and son, and the boy's face.
How the city of Rome itself tells the story of poverty after the war.
after: How much does one job, or one small thing, hold a family together?

title: The Battle of Algiers
why: A recreation of the Algerian fight for independence from France in the 1950s, so realistic that many people thought it was a documentary. It shows the violence of both sides. Militaries and activists have both studied it.
watchFor: The news-reel style of the camera.
How the film gives both the French colonel and the rebels their arguments.
after: When, if ever, is violence justified in fighting for independence? Think about nationalism and its critics.

title: Persepolis
why: Satrapi's memoir of growing up during the Iranian Revolution and the war with Iraq, in striking black-and-white animation. It is funny, angry and personal. It shows big politics through a teenage girl's eyes.
watchFor: How the simple black-and-white drawings handle violence and fear.
Her grandmother, and the advice she gives.
after: How does a revolution feel different to people living through it than in history books?

title: Spirited Away
why: A ten-year-old girl gets trapped in a spirit world and must work in a bathhouse to save her parents. Gorgeous, strange and kind. It won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature.
watchFor: The theme of greed and consumption, from the parents to No-Face.
The polluted river spirit, and Miyazaki's love of nature.
after: What does the film say about work and keeping your name, or yourself?

title: The Worst Person in the World
why: Twelve chapters in the life of Julie, a woman in Oslo approaching thirty who keeps changing career and partner. Funny, honest and romantic about not knowing what you want. A fresh take on the modern coming-of-age story.
watchFor: The scene where time stops in Oslo.
How the chapter titles frame her life.
after: Is it a problem to have many paths, or a freedom?

title: Carol
why: In 1950s New York, a young shop assistant and an elegant, older married woman fall in love. Adapted from Patricia Highsmith, it is shot on film to look like old photographs. Glamorous, careful and full of longing, much like Gatsby's world.
watchFor: Windows, rain and glass between the characters.
Gloves, hands and touch.
after: How did law and social pressure in the 1950s shape who could love whom?

title: Rocks
why: A teenage girl in East London is left to care for her little brother when their mum disappears. The young cast helped write the dialogue, which gives it real energy and humour. A film about friendship holding people up.
watchFor: The phone footage and how the girls see themselves.
The way the school and social services appear.
after: Where would someone in Rocks's position go for help today?

title: Small Axe: Lovers Rock
why: One night at a house party in 1980s West London, among the Black British community. Almost plotless, it is pure atmosphere, music and joy. Part of McQueen's Small Axe series.
watchFor: The long scene of the crowd singing 'Silly Games' with no music.
The threats waiting outside the party.
after: How does a community create safety and joy when the world outside is hostile?

title: Belle
why: Based on Dido Elizabeth Belle, the mixed-race great-niece of Lord Mansfield, raised in an aristocratic family in eighteenth-century England. Her story runs alongside the legal case that shaped the abolition of the slave trade. Inspired by a real painting at Scone Palace.
watchFor: How she is placed, or excluded, at the dinner table.
The painting at the end, and how it was unusual for its time.
after: Think about the art cards: how have portraits shaped who seems to matter in history?

title: The Farewell
why: A Chinese American family keeps a cancer diagnosis secret from their grandmother, staging a fake wedding as an excuse to say goodbye. Based on 'an actual lie' from Wang's own family. Funny and moving about culture and duty.
watchFor: The arguments over whether the lie is kind or cruel.
How Billi feels caught between two cultures.
after: Is it ever right to keep the truth from someone for their own good?

title: Pan's Labyrinth
why: In 1944 Spain, after the Civil War, a girl escapes her cruel fascist stepfather into a dark fairy-tale world. It links fantasy to political violence. Beautifully designed, but scary in parts.
watchFor: The colours: cold blue for the real world and warm gold for the fantasy.
Disobedience, and who chooses it.
after: Is the fantasy real, or her way of resisting? What does fascism do to imagination?

title: Amélie
why: A shy café waitress in Montmartre secretly fixes other people's lives while avoiding her own. Bright and playful, with glowing reds and greens. A light film, but about loneliness underneath.
watchFor: The list of each character's small likes and dislikes.
The strong green and red colour palette.
after: What small kindness could change someone's day?

title: Cinema Paradiso
why: A film director returns to his Sicilian village and remembers growing up in the cinema with the projectionist who became his father figure. A love letter to films and to memory. The final scene is famous for making people cry.
watchFor: The village priest who censors the kissing scenes.
How the cinema mirrors the life of the village over the years.
after: What place shaped you most, and what would you find if you went back?

title: City of God
why: The rise of gangs in a Rio de Janeiro favela over the 1960s to 1980s, told through a boy who wants to become a photographer. Fast, vivid and violent, using many young non-professional actors from the area.
watchFor: How the style changes from warm and golden to cold and chaotic over the decades.
Rocket's camera as a way out.
after: How do poverty and the absence of the state shape what choices are real?

title: Burning
why: A young man meets a childhood acquaintance and her rich, mysterious new friend, and becomes obsessed when she disappears. Based on a Haruki Murakami story. A slow, unsettling mystery about class anger.
watchFor: The sunset dance scene.
What is shown and what is only suggested.
after: Murakami appears on the Japan card. How does the film turn his story into one about Korean class divides?

title: Perfect Days
why: A man who cleans Tokyo's public toilets lives a quiet routine of work, books, music cassettes and photographing trees. Peaceful and meditative, it finds meaning in small things. Kōji Yakusho won Best Actor at Cannes.
watchFor: The light through leaves, called 'komorebi' in Japanese.
His face in the final shot.
after: What would a 'perfect day' look like for you, in very simple terms?

title: 13th
why: The Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery in the US, except as punishment for a crime. DuVernay traces how that exception connects to mass incarceration today. It includes voices from left and right.
watchFor: How the film uses statistics and graphics to build its argument.
Which voices from the other side are included, and how they are presented.
after: What was the strongest point from people the film disagrees with?

title: I Am Not Your Negro
why: Built from James Baldwin's unfinished book about Medgar Evers, Malcolm X and Martin Luther King Jr. Baldwin's words, read by Samuel L. Jackson, are set against archive footage and the present. A brilliant introduction to a brilliant writer.
watchFor: Baldwin's debate at Cambridge and his appearances on television.
How old footage is paired with modern images.
after: Which Baldwin line stayed with you? Save the quote card if it comes up.

title: Exit Through the Gift Shop
why: A French shop owner in LA films street artists, then becomes one himself. Funny and tricky; people still argue about whether it is real. A clever look at art, hype and money.
watchFor: How much of it you believe.
How the art world reacts to Mr Brainwash.
after: What makes something art? Compare it with an artwork from your saved list.

title: Faces Places
why: Agnès Varda, nearly ninety, travels rural France with the young photographer JR, pasting giant portraits of local people on walls, barns and trains. Warm, playful and touching about ageing and friendship.
watchFor: The workers whose faces become part of the landscape.
Varda's failing eyesight and how the film handles it.
after: Whose face would you put on a wall in your town, and why?

title: Man on Wire
why: In 1974, Philippe Petit walked a tightrope between the Twin Towers in New York. Told like a heist film, with reconstructions and real footage. It won the Oscar for Best Documentary.
watchFor: How the film builds suspense when you already know the ending.
The towers themselves, which are never mentioned as gone.
after: What do you think pushes someone to do something so beautiful and so pointless?

title: The Square
why: Follows activists in Tahrir Square from the 2011 revolution through the turbulent years that followed. It shows how hard it is to turn protest into lasting change. Made by an Egyptian American director with people on the ground.
watchFor: The different groups in the square and how they split.
The role of the army.
after: Why do revolutions so often end differently from how they began? Think about populism.

title: Honeyland
why: One of the last wild beekeepers in Europe lives with her mother in a remote village, taking only half the honey. Then a noisy family moves in next door. A small story about sustainability and greed, filmed beautifully.
watchFor: Her rule of 'half for me, half for the bees'.
The natural light: everything was filmed without artificial lighting.
after: What is the environmentalist case made by this film, without any speech?

title: Summer of Soul
why: In 1969, the Harlem Cultural Festival featured Stevie Wonder, Nina Simone, Mahalia Jackson and more, but the footage sat in a basement for fifty years. Joyful and political, about Black pride and music. It won the Oscar for Best Documentary.
watchFor: Nina Simone's performance.
The comparison with Woodstock and whose history gets remembered.
after: Who decides which events become history?

title: Citizenfour
why: Filmed in a Hong Kong hotel room as Edward Snowden reveals mass surveillance by the NSA. Tense and real, it happens in front of the camera. Essential for anyone in governance, risk and privacy.
watchFor: The small paranoid details: the fire alarm, the phone cords.
How the journalists decide what to publish.
after: Where should the line between security and privacy be? Did he do the right thing?

title: Inside Job
why: Explains the 2008 financial crisis: how it happened and who was responsible. Clear and angry, it won the Oscar for Best Documentary. A great way to understand risk, regulation and conflicts of interest.
watchFor: The interviews with economists and how they respond to hard questions.
The links between universities, regulators and banks.
after: What controls might have stopped this? Think like a GRC professional.
